title: MB5-00715
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a 51-year-old registered Palestinian Refugee and permanent resident/passport holder of Syria. He is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant has not presented new evidence and has not requested an oral hearing. The RAD requested additional submissions related to the issue of country conditions in Syria which were received on March 15, 2015.1 DETERMINATION OF THE APPEAL

In this claim, the RPD identifies credibility as the determinative issue. This is to say that, for a number of reasons, the RPD did not believe that the Appellant was at risk of persecution under IRPA s. 96 or at risk for a IRPA s. 97 reason because it concluded that the Appellant did not meet his burden of establishing that his story was true on a balance of probability. I must also identify a determinative issue related to country conditions, which is to say, that the Appellant is not eligible for Canada's protection because he has not established that he faces persecution or a personalized risk, if he returns to Syria, which is in a civil war situation. Therefore, pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention Refugee" pursuant to s. 96 of IRPA nor a "person in need of protection" pursuant to s. 97 of IRPA, but for different reasons.

The Appellant alleges that if he is forced to return to Syria, he will be forced to "join either the militants or the Syrian army (RPD Record, p. 11). The Appellant alleges that Syria is now hell and if he returns there, he will be forced to take sides but because he does not take sides, he will be tortured and/or killed (RPD Record, p. 17).

The Appellant was born in Damascus and has a Palestinian refugee card and Syrian Passport, and according to the documentation, this status is comparable to that of citizenship.2 The Appellant states that he moved to United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 1987 and had been resident there ever since although he states he returned to Syria annually. The Appellant, who has traveled to Canada to visit family on prior occasions, alleges that on this trip to Canada, he felt obligated to remain with his sick and dying mother. As a result, the Appellant alleges that he has now lost his job in UAE and as a consequence, he has lost his right of returning to UAE and he and his family of a wife and five children must now leave UAE to travel to Syria, which is in the midst of a civil war.

After alleging a realization that his situation of having lost his job with no hope of finding another one was clear, the Appellant made a protection claim in Canada in May 2014. The RPD denied this claim in a decision dated (notice of decision) August 8, 2014, whereupon this decision was appealed by submitting a Notice of Appeal, which was received by the RAD on August 26, 2014.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its analysis of the Appellant's credibility because the Appellant's testimony was sufficiently coherent and the provided time lines, in terms of the description of events, approximate what should be considered credible. Therefore, the RPD should have accepted the Appellant's understanding of his own predicament. The Appellant also argues that the documentation is such that the RPD should accept that Appellant cannot return to UAE.
In terms of an outcome from this appeal, the Appellant seeks to be recognized as a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

I note that the RAD has now received Federal Court guidance on the role of the RAD vis-à-vis RPD decisions. Justice Phelan in Huruglica3 states that the RAD "must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection". Justic Phelan goes on to indicate that there is no need for the RAD to enunciate a 'standard of review' and suggests that while the RAD might show some deference on a credibility assessment and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion, in other areas, such as an assessment of country conditions evidence, the RAD need not be deferential.
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE AND FUNCTION OF THE RAD

paragraphs.text: In Njeukam,4 Justice Locke references Huruglica and suggests that "Except in cases where the credibility of a witness is critical or determinative or when the RPD has a particular benefit from the RAD to draw a specific conclusion, the RAD must not give any deference to the analysis of the evidence made by the RPD".

Following Huruglica and Njeukam, I conclude that where in this appeal the issue turns on a question of fact, specifically the RPD's assessment of the credibility of the Appellant when applied to the specific situation of the Appellant, the RPD's determinative credibility assessment must be granted deference and I must provide my own assessment of the evidence. I conclude that in issues which turn on a question of mixed law and fact, specifically the RPD's assessment of country conditions in Syria, I must reach my own conclusion based on my own assessment of the evidence and I do not need to show deference to the RPD's conclusions. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL Core Issue: Did the RPD err in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility and did the RPD err in its conclusion that the Appellant faced persecution if he returns to Syria?

There are elements to the RPD decision which I find persuasive but ultimately the RPD has erred because it focused on the Appellant's situation in the UAE. The Appellant does not have a permanent status in UAE and the temporary status that he had expired on January XXXX, 2015 (RPD Record, p. 56). Put simply, I am unable to speculate or determine the Appellant's current or potential status in UAE. It is possible that the Appellant may be able to return to UAE by application or by some personal appeal. At this point (March 2015), however, the Appellant's only applicable status relates to the fact that he is a registered Palestinian refugee in Syria, which is his country of habitual permanent residence.

What I can conclude with respect to the Appellant's allegations related to UAE, is that I am in agreement with the RPD's conclusion on the Appellant's credibility. This is to say, that the Appellant chose to fall out of status in UAE, assuming he has fallen out of status, and forced this situation where he places himself at risk of return to Syria. I note that the Appellant makes arguments that his family, who live in UAE, is likewise at risk. Again, I must conclude that these are the Appellant's decisions and the RAD cannot analyze or speculate on the disposition of the Appellant's family nor can their fate be a factor in this decision.

With respect to the RPD's determinative decision on the Appellant's credibility, the RPD finds that the Appellant misrepresents his risk in the sense that he applied for Canada's protection before he had confirmed that he had lost his job. In fact, the RPD shows that the Appellant is applying for protection during a period when, during testimony, he likely still had his job. Specifically, the Appellant stated that he last talked with his boss in early May 2014, and was told that he "might be losing his job", if he did not return (Oral Hearing at minute 1:03). The Appellant was asked if he knew he had lost his job at that point and the Appellant stated that he was "hoping for the best" and that he had not spoken to his boss after this occasion (Oral Hearing at minute 1:06).

The RPD states that: You testified that you applied for refugee protection after finding out that you had lost your job in the UAE because you believed at that point you were in danger of having to return to Syria. I did not find your evidence pertaining to you losing your job in the UAE as credible. You initially testified that you found out you had lost your job in early June despite the fact that your Basis of Claim Form (BOC) was signed on May 20, 2014. Your testimony on this subject changed. Later in your testimony you stated that you came to believe that you had lost your job after speaking with your friend XXXX between the dates of May 20 and May 26, 2014. Your explanation for this contradiction was that early June was when you had sent your wife to your employer to obtain documents proving you had lost your job for you to show it to your lawyer. You testified that your wife did not perform this task because when she contacted your employer she was requested to bring the family passports with her to that office so that the residency permits could be cancelled. She was, scared of the consequences of this and therefor did not attend as your employer had requested. You testified that it was the date on which your wife had contacted your employer in early June as when you became one hundred percent sure that you had lost your job (RPD Decision, p. 2).

The basic RPD conclusion is that the Appellant could still travel to UAE (RPD decision dated in late July 2014) and perhaps seek a new job or perhaps get his old job back. The RPD goes on to conclude that the Appellant was "likely still" employed, which would make the Appellant's claim for Canada's protection a fraudulent effort to secure a status in Canada.

The Appellant reviews the testimony to argue that the RPD should not take this perspective because it is possible that in this time line the Appellant did in fact become certain that he had lost his job prior to making a protection claim (i.e., prior to signing forms on May 20, 2014) (Appellant's Memorandum of Argument, paragraph 6).

The Appellant also argues that the RPD should take into consideration that the Appellant has a lower education and that he comes from a different culture and that it would be microscopically inspecting the evidence, and thus unwarranted, to reach an adverse credibility conclusion.

I cannot accept this argument. Setting aside the basic reality that the Appellant could have returned to UAE and gone directly to the 'general administration' of his employer to try and get his job back or perhaps gone and secured another job, the Appellant is 51, which is not old by any criteria. Given what is at stake, the actions of the Appellant are not credible. In addition, the efforts of the Appellant to secure proof of his dismissal, as noted by the RPD, are not credible. The Appellant states he is in contact with his wife daily (via VIBER - Oral Hearing at minute 1:09) and has contacted a co-worker, identified as 'XXXX, on several occasions. The Appellant alleges that he phoned this co-worker to find out his status and this co-worker relayed the information that he was told that the Appellant's immediate supervisor could do nothing and that this co-worker should "go to the general administration" to find out more or make representation on the Appellant's behalf (Oral Hearing at minute 1:14). At this point, the Appellant alleges that he "gave up" and "did not follow up" (Oral Hearing at minute 1:15). As a result, the Appellant can produce no supporting evidence of being terminated by his employer.

I must conclude that the RPD is well within its area of discretion to view all this as lacking in credibility given the open communications lines to his wife and co-worker, the potential to secure documents by electronic means and the alleged manifest importance of being dismissed.

Although I am in agreement with the RPD that at the time of its decision the Appellant's allegation, that his situation for remaining in UAE was hopeless such that return was impossible, was not credible, I must also recognize that time has now passed and that perhaps the Appellant now has lost the capacity to return to UAE. This being the case, I must conclude that the Appellant has manufactured this risk of return to Syria (self-induced refugee status) and this initiative is incompatible with principles of Canada's refugee protection regime. According to Justice Snider in a Federal Court decision involving a Cuban national: [13] The Federal Court of Appeal decision in Valentin, above, is directly applicable to this application. Valentin bars self-induced refugee status. It starts from the premise that a claimant has a valid exit visa. It then bars the claimant from overstaying the visa and relying on the self-created overstay as a ground of persecution. In this case, the Applicant held a valid exit visa. She failed to renew her permit, as she could have done. She cannot rely on self-created overstay as a ground of persecution. Valentin has been consistently followed in this Court where the facts are similar to those before me; see for example, Jassi v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 356, [2010] F.C.J No. 412 (QL). [14] The jurisprudence is to a similar effect in the context of a s. 97 claim for protection. In Zandi v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 411, [2004] F.C.J. No. 503 (QL), Justice Kelen considered the situation of an Iranian who defected to Canada while here for an athletic competition. In considering whether the claimant could claim protection on the basis that he would be punished for defecting on his return to Iran, Justice Kelen stated as follows: To paraphrase the Federal Court of Appeal in Valentin, supra, a defector cannot gain legal status in Canada under IRPA by creating a "need for protection" under section 97 of IRPA by freely, of their own accord and with no reason, making themselves liable to punishment by violating a law of general application in their home country about complying with exit visas, i.e. returning. [15] In short, the jurisprudence is clear that the Applicant, who failed to renew her valid exit visa, cannot rely on the possibility of punishment under Cuba's Criminal Code as grounds for protection under s. 96 or s. 97.5

The next element of analysis must be the risk that the Appellant faces in Syria. On this question, I find the RPD erred in its substantive conclusion. The RPD concludes with respect to return to Syria that: Based on my readings of the country condition documents, I am satisfied that if you were to be returned to Syria you would face more than a mere possibility of being persecuted due to your Palestinian nationality. Accordingly, if I were to find that the Government of the UAE were to send you back to Syria, you would have a well founded fear of persecution in that country as well (RPD Decision, p. 2).

I note that the RPD did not provide any substantive analysis to support this conclusion. Although I recognize that Syria is in the midst of a civil war and simply being in Syria is dangerous, this does not mean that the Appellant himself is at risk of persecution or faces a personalized risk of being harmed.

My understanding of the documentation is that Palestinian refugees in Syria are not aligned with any side in the civil war. In fact, they are viewed as have made efforts to avoid getting involved. According to one source: Sources indicate that most Palestinians tried to avoid engaging in the conflict (AP 26 July 2012; UN [June 2013], 3), but this neutrality has "come under huge pressure with the conflict increasingly penetrating their communities" (ibid.). According to media sources, some Palestinians are supporting the government and some are supporting the opposition (Le Monde 3 Jan. 2013; Le Figaro 17 Dec. 2012).6

I note that the Appellant himself confirms this interpretation when asked if he had taken a side in the Syrian civil war, he responded that he had tried to "stay neutral" (Oral Hearing at minute 1:33). I note that in his BOC, the Appellant notes that he did his 'mandatory' military service in the infantry, completed in 1987 (RPD Record, p. 46). I do not see any allegation or mention during the hearing that he might be required to serve in the military. At 51 years old, with many children, this is not normally an age where individuals are required to serve and I see no evidence of men of a similar profile as the Appellant being pressed into service by any group.

I also note that the Appellant identifies having built a home in XXXX, Syria, and that these photos show damage (RPD Record, p. 112). This is obviously not good because beginning in February 2014, this whole area became a major battle zone where the Syrian army has fought pitched battles with such groups as Jabhat Al-Nusra and Ahrar Al Sham.

I note that the risk identified by the Appellant is that Syria is simply dangerous and that "camps are hit" and that he has friends that were killed in the violence. I must conclude that this is consistent with the documentation on general state of insecurity and risk that exists in Syria. According to one source speaking specifically about Palestinian refugees in Syria, The Professor of Middle Eastern History stated that Palestinians in Syria are targeted by both sides in the conflict (19 June 2013). An article in the Irish Times, a newspaper founded in Ireland in 1859 (Irish Times n.d.), cites Palestinians living in Syria who allege that Free Syrian Army fighters attack, rob, and arrest them at checkpoints, and that the regime's army also arrest them at checkpoints and that the government bombed a mosque in Yarmouk in December 2012 (ibid. 21 May 2013).7

I note that the Appellant at no time in his answers to questions related to facing a risk in Syria mentions a specific refugee Convention related risk or a specific agent of persecution. In fact, quite the opposite. The Appellant notes, in contrast to the difficulty of living in UAE, that he had just completed building a house in Syria and that education was free and healthcare was free and that overall it was accommodating and easy to live there (Oral Hearing at minute 48).

I must conclude that this is a situation of civil war and that in this case, the Appellant does not have a profile of belonging to a group of people or being an individual who have been targeted for one of the criteria identified in the Refugee Convention. With respect to a s. 97(1) risk, I must conclude that the Appellant faces a generalized risk as a result of the existence of a civil war in Syria in which all individuals face this same risk. Using a non-comparative approach and considering the Appellant's specific situation, the Appellant is simply an individual who would be caught in the cross-fire of a wide spread, dangerous and destructive civil war, if he were to return to Syria. The Appellant is not known as an individual who is sought or targeted in Syria. The Appellant is a Palestinian, which is a group whose members might be a targeted for essentially criminal reasons (e.g., robbery) but which, as a group, has not picked sides nor is perceived to have picked sides in this conflict.

I note that in an additional submission the Appellant argues that the plight of Palestinians in Syria should be viewed as persecution based on 'race and ethnic background': National Documentation Package 13.2 further states on Page 7 that "displaced Palestinians have experienced a disproportionate levels of destruction of Palestinian homes". This clearly shows that Palestinians have been specifically targeted around Syria and have become victims of specific persecution due to their Race and ethnic background. What is even more troubling is the fact that Palestinians seeking assistance for refugee protection in neighboring countries have also become victims of persecution. The article : The Vulnerability of Palestinian refugees from Syria (copy attached) clearly shows that again Palestinians who were once partially independent in Syria prior to the conflict have now been crumbled, leaving them largely dependent on UNRWA and funding from the international community.8

In reviewing Tab 13.29 I must conclude that this article does not support the logic advanced by the Appellant. This section reads: According to an UNRWA needs assessment undertaken in October 2013, Damascus city and suburbs host the largest number of displaced Palestinians and has experienced disproportionate levels of destruction of Palestinian homes. Palestinians displaced within Syria traditionally stay in or near pre-existing Palestinian communities. Hence, the vast majority remain concentrated in Damascus city and suburbs (200,000 IDPs), followed by smaller pockets in Aleppo (6,600), Dar'a (13,100), Homs (6,500), Hama (3,100) and Lattakia (4,500).

The thrust of this quote is that because Palestinians are in strategic areas (the approaches to the capital Damascus) they have be disproportionately 'affected' (their homes destroyed) in combat related activity. The point is that this article and the article provided by the Appellant in his 'additional comments' provide evidence of 'vulnerability', which is to say exposure to danger and a "deterioration of the material conditions", which means that as they are forced to flee they are having difficulty securing housing and food.10 Put simply, these are conditions related to a generalized risk for any and every one in Syria at this time. With respect to the treatment of Palestinians in the surrounding countries, this is not an issue because Canada is not going to return the Appellant to any surrounding country.

My conclusion that the Appellant faces a generalized risk, if he were to return to Syria, is reached after considering the Chairperson's Guidelines concerning Civilian Non-Combatants Fearing Persecution in Civil War Situations and with specific reference to how these are impacted by the new category of "Person in Need of Protection" in IRPA.

For all these reasons, I confirm the determination of the RPD, but for different reasons. In my analysis of all of the evidence, I conclude the appellant is not at risk in Syria under s. 96 or s. 97 of IRPA. I also conclude the Appellant cannot return to the UAE. I conclude Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection".

Therefore, the appeal is dismissed. Stephen J. Gallagher Stephen J. Gallagher April 17, 2015 Date /cl 1 Me S.
